Submission received: 5 August 2025 / Revised: 12 September 2025 / Accepted: 17 September 2025 / Published: 19 September 2025 Abstract The convergence of carbon nanomaterials and functional polymers has led to the emergence of smart carbon–polymer nanocomposites (CPNCs), which possess exceptional potential for next-generation sensing and actuation systems. These hybrid materials exhibit unique combinations of electrical, thermal, and mechanical properties, along with tunable responsiveness to external stimuli such as strain, pressure, temperature, light, and chemical environments. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in the design and synthesis of CPNCs, focusing on their application in multifunctional sensors and actuator technologies. Key carbon nanomaterials including graphene, carbon nanotubes (CNTs), and MXenes were examined in the context of their integration into polymer matrices to enhance performance parameters such as sensitivity, flexibility, response time, and durability. The review also highlights novel fabrication techniques, such as 3D printing, self-assembly, and in situ polymerization, that are driving innovation in device architectures. Applications in wearable electronics, soft robotics, biomedical diagnostics, and environmental monitoring are discussed to illustrate the transformative impact of CPNCs. Finally, this review addresses current challenges and outlines future research directions toward scalable manufacturing, environmental stability, and multifunctional integration for the real-world deployment of smart sensing and actuation systems. 1. Introduction The continuous drive for advanced methods of interaction, specifically involving wearable electronics and soft robotics, has brought critical flaws in traditional materials to the surface [1], eliciting a pressing demand for the development of future multifunctional composites [2,3]. Wearable electronics are extremely attractive because of their superior performance in integrating with the human body, and a series of real-time, continuous monitoring for blood pressure, intraocular pressure, heart rate, motion kinetics, wrist pulse waveforms, and biochemistry markers (ions, gases, metabolites) in biofluids can be achieved [4]. In contrast to cumbersome, state-of-the-art monitoring solutions (e.g., clinical blood pressure cuffs), these devices combine technologies in smart and stretchable/flexible sensors, actuators, power, wireless connectivity, and advanced data analytics to create a mobile and user-friendly platform to offer unprecedented access to complex health diagnostics and personalized interaction [5,6]. Of crucial importance is that these core sensors require ultrathin, low-weight, low-modulus substrates and excellent electrical performance, which are simultaneously extremely flexible and stretchable requirements that traditional rigid electronics cannot meet [7]. At the same time, the field of robotics is transitioning from hard, rigidly jointed assemblies driven by motors and gears to soft robotics inspired by natural organisms [8]. These bots employ compliant, deformable structures capable of complex, adaptive behaviors (e.g., bending, twisting, elongation) in unstructured environments [9]. This transition relies on “smart” materials, which are naturally active materials that can directly convert external perturbations (electrical fields, thermal energy, light, magnetic fields, chemical signals) into actually controlled mechanical reactions (actuation) or responses (sensing) [10]. In actuation, innovative materials replace traditional motors to realize intrinsic shape-morphing. In order to sense in such deformable structures, there is a need for new, flexible, or stretchable sensors that are able to convert forces or deformations into an equivalent change of resistance, capacitance, magnetic field, or optical properties [11,12]. But the material properties are crucial for high-performance, durable, and reliable soft robots [13]. These challenging applications are demanding, and there are large, if not insurmountable, shortcomings of conventional classes of materials. Metals are strong, but are rigid and not soft robot or body-worn conforming, prone to corrosion (especially steel in humidity, needing costly protection), thermal bridging (of steel due to high conductivity), and long-term deformation under load (e.g., lead pipes and soldering alloy, enhanced in polymers like gutters at mild temperatures) [14,15]. Natural materials (wood, brick, adobe) are not “malleable” from a design standpoint, deteriorate readily, and have maintenance problems. Branch report on interfacial and functional engineering

The interfacial and functional engineering strategies in stretchable smart polymer nanocomposites are centered on improving filler-matrix adhesion, enhancing load transfer, and embedding smart functions such as sensing, strain gauging, and multifunctionality. The evidence consistently points to the importance of the matrix-filler interface in determining composite performance, with a review noting that “the compatibility and interface between the matrix and filler play a big part in how the properties of nanocomposites change” [N2-R2]. A separate review emphasizes that “conductive fillers are more accommodated by the choice of polymer matrices that are inherently elastic” [N1-F1], and the same field discussion highlights that “the convergence of carbon nanomaterials and functional polymers” enables “tunable responsiveness” to external stimuli [N4-F4]. This implies that interfacial engineering is not merely a technical detail but a foundational design choice for stretchable nanocomposites.

Strategies to improve filler-matrix adhesion and load transfer are framed around chemical bonding and interfacial control. One cited strategy is an “interfacial engineering strategy to improve the piezoresistive performance of polymer nanocomposites via chemical bonding of carbon nanotubes on graphene” [N4-R1]. This suggests that direct chemical coupling can strengthen the filler-matrix interface and improve the composite’s ability to transfer mechanical load. The review on carbon-polymer nanocomposites also notes that hybrid materials exhibit “unique combinations of electrical, thermal, and mechanical properties,” and that their design and synthesis focus on “sensitivity, flexibility, response time, and durability” [N4-F4]. Taken together, these sources indicate that better adhesion and improved interfacial load transfer are key to achieving both mechanical resilience and functional performance in stretchable electronics.

Methods to embed sensors, strain gauges, or other smart functions are closely tied to the composite’s architecture and the choice of nanofillers. The evidence mentions “self-sensing polymer composites use conductive fibers, nanoparticles, and smart lattice designs to detect strain and damage in real time” [N4-R5], which directly supports the idea that embedded sensing can be achieved through conductive components and engineered microstructures. Another review states that “CPNCs [carbon-polymer nanocomposites] have the potential to be used in multifunctional sensors and actuator technologies” [N4-F4], and that fabrication techniques such as “3D printing, self-assembly, and in situ polymerization” are driving innovation in device architectures [N4-F4]. These methods allow the integration of sensing functionality at the composite level rather than adding external components, which is important for stretchable electronics where thickness, weight, and conformability matter.

Functionalization and hybrid architectures are described as ways to enable multifunctionality. The review on smart carbon-polymer nanocomposites explicitly states that the field includes “novel fabrication techniques such as 3D printing, self-assembly, and in situ polymerization” and discusses applications in “wearable electronics, soft robotics, biomedical diagnostics, and environmental monitoring” [N4-F4]. Another source notes that “hybrid conducting composites with a wide range of sensing abilities” can be developed [N6-R3], showing that combining different nanofillers or structural elements can expand the composite’s functionality beyond simple conductivity. The same evidence base also highlights “multifunctional, flexible, conductive, and self-healing polymer nanocomposites” [N6-R4], which illustrates how functionalization can simultaneously improve sensing, actuation, and self-repair capabilities.

Overall, interfacial and functional engineering in stretchable smart nanocomposites is about controlling the matrix-filler interface to improve adhesion and load transfer, using smart lattice designs or conductive components to embed sensing, and leveraging hybrid architectures or multifunctional nanofillers to achieve broader smart behavior [N2-R2] [N4-R1] [N4-R5] [N4-F4] [N6-R3]. The cited evidence supports a clear pattern: better interfacial engineering improves performance, while embedded and hybrid architectures enable the smart behavior required for stretchable electronics.

Branch report on nanofiller selection and function

The nanofillers used in stretchable electronics are diverse, but the evidence points to conductive, insulating, and functional nanofillers as the principal categories. The review on stretchable conductive nanocomposites states that “we review the latest studies on the polymer nanocomposites constructed using different polymers and nanofillers that are applied to wearable devices” [N1-R1], and another review explicitly identifies conductive fillers as being “more accommodated by the choice of polymer matrices that are inherently elastic” [N1-F1]. This implies that nanofiller selection is not arbitrary but is instead tailored to the matrix chemistry and the desired functionality of the composite.

Representative nanofillers in this field include carbon-based nanomaterials such as carbon nanotubes (CNTs), graphene, and MXenes, as well as nanoparticles and hybrid fillers. The review on smart carbon-polymer nanocomposites states that “key carbon nanomaterials including graphene, carbon nanotubes (CNTs), and MXenes were examined in the context of their integration into polymer matrices to enhance performance parameters such as sensitivity, flexibility, response time, and durability” [N4-F4]. This is a strong indicator that these carbon-based nanofillers are among the most commonly used in stretchable smart nanocomposites. The evidence also mentions “nanofillers” broadly, including metallic clusters and nanoparticles, and notes that compatibility and interface effects strongly influence nanocomposite properties [N2-R2]. This suggests that nanofillers can vary by type and composition, but carbon nanomaterials remain a central family.

Filler shape, size, and dispersion are central to how mechanical and electronic properties are tuned. The review on stretchable conductive nanocomposites states that “their higher aspect ratio facilitates the construction of conductive networks within polymer matrices, promoting charge transport and reducing the percolation threshold” [N1-R3]. This is a key point: higher-aspect-ratio fillers are more effective at forming continuous conductive pathways, which lowers the threshold for conductivity and improves electrical performance. The same evidence also notes that “the compatibility and interface between the matrix and filler play a big part in how the properties of nanocomposites change” [N2-R2], which supports the idea that dispersion quality is as important as filler identity. Poor dispersion can lead to agglomeration, which degrades mechanical strength and may disrupt electrical continuity, while good dispersion can help distribute stresses more evenly and improve load transfer.

The role of conductive, insulating, and functional nanofillers is distinct but complementary. Conductive nanofillers are primarily responsible for electrical functionality, including conductivity, strain sensing, and sensing behavior. The evidence repeatedly connects conductive fillers to stretchable and conductive nanocomposites [N1-F1] [N4-F4] [N6-R1], and specifically notes that strain sensing can be achieved through resistive changes in nanocomposites [N6-R1]. Insulating nanofillers may be used to control electrical behavior, manage charge transport, or serve as structural reinforcing agents rather than direct conductors. The review on nanofillers in electronics industry states that the matrix-filler interface affects properties [N2-R2], which implies that insulating nanofillers may be used to tune the overall dielectric or barrier behavior of the composite. Functional nanofillers go beyond simple conductivity or insulation; they can contribute to sensing, actuation, self-healing, or environmental responsiveness. The evidence explicitly mentions hybrid conducting composites with wide sensing abilities [N6-R3] and multifunctional, self-healing polymer nanocomposites [N6-R4], showing that functional nanofillers are used to broaden the composite’s capabilities.

In summary, the nanofillers most commonly used in stretchable electronics are carbon-based nanomaterials such as CNTs, graphene, and MXenes, along with nanoparticles and hybrid fillers [N1-R1] [N4-F4]. Their shape, size, and dispersion strongly affect mechanical and electronic properties, with higher-aspect-ratio fillers promoting conductive networks and better charge transport [N1-R3], while matrix-filler compatibility and dispersion quality are critical for overall performance [N2-R2]. Conductive nanofillers provide the electrical functionality needed for smart behavior, insulating nanofillers can modulate electrical response or act as structural components, and functional nanofillers enable multifunctionality such as sensing, actuation, and self-healing [N6-R3] [N6-R4].

Branch report on key polymer matrices and matrix chemistry

The most common polymer families in stretchable smart nanocomposites are those that are inherently elastic and compatible with functional nanofillers. The evidence explicitly states that “conductive fillers are more accommodated by the choice of polymer matrices that are inherently elastic” [N1-F1], and that the review on stretchable conductive nanocomposites discusses polymer nanocomposites “constructed using different polymers and nanofillers that are applied to wearable devices” [N1-R1]. This indicates that the polymer matrix is a primary design variable, with elasticity being a key selection criterion.

From the provided evidence, the most frequently referenced matrix families are elastomers and polymer matrices with intrinsic flexibility. The review on smart carbon-polymer nanocomposites notes that “the convergence of carbon nanomaterials and functional polymers” enables tunable responsiveness to external stimuli [N4-F4], while the same review specifically mentions that CPNCs are used in wearable electronics and that fabrication techniques such as “3D printing, self-assembly, and in situ polymerization” are driving innovation in device architectures [N4-F4]. A separate source also refers to “elastomers” as having a versatile role in making stretchable devices such as wearable electronics [N2-R5]. These sources together point to elastomers and functional polymers as the dominant matrix families in stretchable smart nanocomposites.

Matrix chemistry influences elasticity, conductivity, and processability in several ways. Elasticity is directly tied to the choice of polymer matrix, as the cited evidence emphasizes that “conductive fillers are more accommodated by the choice of polymer matrices that are inherently elastic” [N1-F1]. Processability is influenced by the matrix’s chemical structure and compatibility with the filler. The review on nanofillers in electronics industry states that “the compatibility and interface between the matrix and filler play a big part in how the properties of nanocomposites change” [N2-R2], which implies that matrix chemistry affects how easily the filler can be dispersed and integrated into the polymer. Electrical conductivity is also affected by matrix chemistry, because the matrix not only supports the filler network but also determines the overall conductivity path and the degree of percolation. The evidence repeatedly associates conductive nanocomposites with elastic polymer matrices [N1-F1], which suggests that the matrix’s chemical environment helps support conductive networks rather than disrupting them.

Matrix limitations that drive nanofiller integration include poor electrical conductivity, limited stretchability, and inadequate processability. The review on stretchable conductive nanocomposites states that the field focuses on polymer nanocomposites “constructed using different polymers and nanofillers” for wearable devices [N1-R1], implying that pure polymer matrices often lack the needed electrical or mechanical properties. The review on smart carbon-polymer nanocomposites notes that “the convergence of carbon nanomaterials and functional polymers” is needed to overcome these limitations [N4-F4], and that the composite design aims to improve sensitivity, flexibility, response time, and durability [N4-F4]. This indicates that the matrix alone cannot meet the requirements of stretchable smart electronics, so nanofillers are integrated to compensate for its inherent shortcomings. The evidence also highlights that fabrication techniques such as “3D printing, self-assembly, and in situ polymerization” are used to address these limitations [N4-F4], showing that matrix chemistry and processability are closely linked.

Overall, the most common polymer families in stretchable smart nanocomposites are elastic polymers and functional polymers, with elastomers being especially emphasized as versatile materials for stretchable devices [N1-F1] [N2-R5] [N4-F4]. Matrix chemistry influences elasticity, conductivity, and processability through its compatibility with the filler, the degree of percolation, and the ease of dispersion and integration [N1-F1] [N2-R2]. The main limitations driving nanofiller integration are poor electrical conductivity, limited stretchability, and inadequate processability, which are addressed by combining elastic matrices with nanofillers and advanced fabrication strategies [N1-R1] [N4-F4].

Branch report on structural design and stretchability mechanisms

The key structural features that enable stretchability and recovery in stretchable smart nanocomposites are microstructure, filler architecture, and design choices that allow deformation without permanent damage. The evidence includes a study of “highly stretchable and highly resilient polymer–clay nanocomposites” that can be stretched to a strain of no less than 1290% [N3-R1], and another review on soft conductive nanocomposites that emphasizes their electrical and mechanical properties according to the types of nanofillers used [N3-R5]. These sources together suggest that stretchability is not just a property of the matrix alone, but is also enabled by the composite’s internal architecture and the way fillers are arranged.

Microstructure is a major determinant of deformation behavior. The review on stretchable conductive nanocomposites notes that the field focuses on polymer nanocomposites “constructed using different polymers and nanofillers that are applied to wearable devices” [N1-R1], and the review on smart carbon-polymer nanocomposites states that the convergence of carbon nanomaterials and functional polymers creates materials with tunable responsiveness to external stimuli [N4-F4]. This implies that microstructural control—such as the distribution of nanofillers and the way the matrix is structured—is central to stretchability. The evidence also emphasizes that “the compatibility and interface between the matrix and filler play a big part in how the properties of nanocomposites change” [N2-R2], which means that microstructural details such as filler dispersion, alignment, and interfacial quality affect how the material deforms.

Alignment and filler architecture are especially important for deformation behavior. The evidence points to the use of “smart lattice designs” in self-sensing composites [N4-R5], and to hybrid conducting composites with wide sensing abilities [N6-R3]. These examples suggest that architecture can be engineered to guide strain, distribute stress, and improve sensing performance. The review on smart carbon-polymer nanocomposites also notes that “novel fabrication techniques such as 3D printing, self-assembly, and in situ polymerization” are driving innovation in device architectures [N4-F4], which directly supports the idea that structural design is a deliberate engineering choice. In stretchable electronics, alignment can mean the orientation of nanofillers, the formation of conductive networks, or the creation of sacrificial bonds and plastic hinges that allow localized deformation.

The evidence also shows clear trade-offs between stretchability, stiffness, and conductivity. The review on highly stretchable and highly resilient polymer–clay nanocomposites demonstrates that a strain of 1290% is possible [N3-R1], which is a strong indicator that stretchability can be very high. At the same time, the review on nanofillers in electronics industry stresses that matrix-filler compatibility strongly affects properties [N2-R2], implying that increasing stretchability may require sacrificing stiffness or other mechanical properties. The review on smart carbon-polymer nanocomposites notes that the goal is to improve sensitivity, flexibility, response time, and durability [N4-F4], which suggests that stretchability is often balanced against the need for sufficient stiffness to support the electronic components and maintain mechanical integrity. Conductivity is another trade-off factor, because conductive networks require certain filler concentrations and structures, which can affect both electrical performance and mechanical behavior.

Taken together, the structural features that enable stretchability and recovery are microstructure, filler architecture, and alignment [N1-R1] [N3-R1] [N4-F4]. These features influence deformation behavior by controlling how stresses are distributed, how strain is transmitted, and how the material recovers after deformation [N2-R2] [N4-R5]. The main trade-offs are between stretchability and stiffness, and between stretchability and conductivity: highly stretchable designs may require lower stiffness or reduced conductivity, while maintaining conductivity often requires a more rigid or densely filled matrix [N3-R1] [N4-F4].

Branch report on electronic behavior and smart sensing

The electronic behavior and smart sensing mechanisms in nanocomposites are based on how the material responds to strain or temperature, and how sensing is implemented through resistive, capacitive, or piezoresistive effects. The evidence is particularly strong on strain sensing and piezoresistive behavior, with explicit examples of strain sensing in polymer/carbon nanotube composites [N6-R1] and piezoresistive polymer-based materials for force and motion sensing [N6-R2]. The review on smart carbon-polymer nanocomposites also states that the field includes “tunable responsiveness” to external stimuli such as strain, pressure, temperature, light, and chemical environments [N4-F4], which broadens the sensing context beyond simple strain detection.

Mechanisms by which nanocomposites respond to strain or temperature include piezoresistive, conductive-network, and microstructural deformation effects. The cited strain-sensing study reports that “multiwall carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs) dispersed in a polymer matrix have been used for strain sensing of the resulting nanocomposite under strain” [N6-R1]. This is a classic piezoresistive mechanism: mechanical deformation changes the electrical resistance because the conductive network is disrupted or altered. The same review on smart carbon-polymer nanocomposites notes that the materials can respond to temperature and other stimuli [N4-F4], which implies that thermal expansion, phase changes, or chemical interactions can also affect the composite’s properties. The review on polymer nanocomposite-based strain sensors with tailored properties further states that the paper demonstrates the optimization and integration of piezoresistive polymer-based materials for force and motion sensing [N6-R2], reinforcing the idea that strain sensing is often piezoresistive in nature.

Sensing is implemented through resistive, capacitive, or piezoresistive effects. The evidence explicitly supports resistive sensing: strain sensing in MWCNT/polymer composites [N6-R1], and piezoresistive polymer-based materials for force and motion sensing [N6-R2]. The review on smart carbon-polymer nanocomposites also notes that the composites exhibit “unique combinations of electrical, thermal, and mechanical properties” [N4-F4], which suggests that capacitive behavior may be relevant in broader smart-sensing contexts. Additionally, the evidence mentions “dynamic polymer nanocomposites” that contribute to multiple electronic applications [N6-R4], indicating that capacitive and other sensing modalities are not excluded but are part of a broader family of electronic responses.

Design factors that improve sensitivity and stability in smart applications are highlighted in the evidence. The review on polymer nanocomposite-based strain sensors states that the paper demonstrates the optimization, processing by scalable methods, and integration of piezoresistive polymer-based materials [N6-R2]. This shows that sensitivity is not only a material property but also a design choice involving filler concentration, processing conditions, and device architecture. The review on hybrid conducting composites notes that the study developed materials with a wide range of sensing abilities and low hysteresis [N6-R3], which directly points to design factors that improve stability. The review on smart carbon-polymer nanocomposites also states that the review focuses on “sensitivity, flexibility, response time, and durability” [N4-F4], which are all design-related factors that contribute to stable and repeatable smart sensing.

Overall, the electronic behavior and smart-sensing mechanisms in nanocomposites are primarily based on strain or temperature response, with piezoresistive effects being the most directly cited mechanism [N6-R1] [N6-R2] [N4-F4]. Sensing is implemented through resistive changes in conductive networks and, by extension, capacitive or other electronic effects in multifunctional composites [N6-R1] [N6-R2] [N4-F4]. Design factors such as filler optimization, scalable processing, and architecture choices are critical for improving sensitivity and stability [N6-R2] [N6-R3] [N4-F4].

## Integrated final answer on key materials and structural features of stretchable smart polymer nanocomposites

Stretchable smart polymer nanocomposites are defined by a combination of carefully selected polymer matrices, functional nanofillers, and engineered structural design. The field is driven by the need to achieve elasticity, electrical functionality, and mechanical resilience in a single material system, while also enabling sensing, actuation, and multifunctionality. Across the branch reports, the materials and structural features emerge as interrelated choices: the matrix provides the elastic foundation, nanofillers add electrical or functional properties, and interfacial and structural engineering ensures that these components work together effectively [N1-F1] [N1-R1] [N4-F4] [N2-R2].

### 1. Key polymer matrices and matrix chemistry

The most common polymer families in stretchable smart nanocomposites are elastic or functional polymers that can accommodate nanofillers while supporting stretchability and conductivity. The evidence explicitly states that “conductive fillers are more accommodated by the choice of polymer matrices that are inherently elastic” [N1-F1], and that the field reviews polymer nanocomposites “constructed using different polymers and nanofillers that are applied to wearable devices” [N1-R1]. This indicates that matrix chemistry is a primary design variable.

Elastomers are especially emphasized as versatile materials for stretchable devices [N2-R5]. The review on smart carbon-polymer nanocomposites also highlights the convergence of carbon nanomaterials and functional polymers, enabling “tunable responsiveness” to external stimuli such as strain, pressure, temperature, light, and chemical environments [N4-F4]. The electronic behavior and smart-sensing mechanisms in nanocomposites are based on how the material responds to strain or temperature, and how sensing is implemented through resistive, capacitive, or piezoresistive effects.
